Experiments / sun-5

The sun world, fifth start halted

A new start under rules 7 - the machine is the universe. Every processor and every graphics card is a world of its own, seven of them joined in a ring, and the light of each is the electricity its device really draws. There is no day and no year. Signals are sometimes read wrong, and an organism can store energy in its own body.

This world stands still: none of its seven nodes is running. Rig A's three nodes were stopped cleanly and have stood still since Nov 13 13:31 UTC; rig B's four nodes were stopped cleanly and have stood still since Nov 13 13:34 UTC. The journal's entry of Nov 13 13:35 UTC: “The fifth start is stopped cleanly and kept; a test of a pi oracle runs on the five cards”. The numbers here are those of each band's last round.

What it is

Rules 6 took the pay for tasks away. Rules 7 take the hand-set sky away. A node of the world is no longer a machine but one device of a machine: its processor, or one of its graphics cards. Each has a band of land with its own founder and its own clan, and the seven bands close into a ring, so an organism that travels east out of a processor's band arrives in a card's.

The light of a band is what its device draws, read every round: a card through its own meter, a processor through its energy counter. A busy world makes its own sun brighter, up to the device's full power, and an idle device leaves its world in twilight. Warmth is the device's temperature. There is no day, no night by the clock and no year: it is dark where the supply drops.

So the world has a size for the first time: 560 columns by 512 rows, 286,720 regions, as many as the cards have room for and the processors can light.

Two things are new in the land. Calls, marks, smells and tremors are sometimes read wrong, more often the weaker they are and the hotter the device. And an organism can store energy in its own body and draw it back, at a loss of a quarter.

The plant founder is not used: in the fourth start its line never left its first region.

How it was started

The owner asked for it on 2026-11-12, after the fourth start had ended with an outage, and said it should use both machines. Before the start: the engines agreed with the rules in every mode and gave the golden record, written anew for rules 7; a native build under sanitizers agreed byte for byte; the tests of rules 7, of rules 6 and of the senses passed and no cheat worked; all five graphics cards gave the same world as the processors; the three devices of one machine ran together for 28 minutes with their real meters, and their regions stayed small enough for the cards (2 of 18,829 too large on the richest band); and all seven nodes were started, stopped and resumed on test data through the very scripts that run the world. Each node has a guard beside it that stops it cleanly if its machine runs out of memory or loses its network, which is what ended the fourth start.

Not done before the start: a run with every band full at full power. The longest trial ended with the bands half full.

How it will be read

Against the fourth start where the numbers still mean the same. The days, years and seasons of the earlier pages do not exist here: what they showed is now the draw, the temperature and the load of each device.

Over time

The seven bands against the time, the one axis they share: each counts its own rounds, at its own pace. From the timed readings, one a minute for each band. Marks are the journal's starts, stops, restarts, deploys and crashes; point at one to read it. After a restart a band's line dips for a few rounds, while its node counts its organisms as it reads its regions in.

By round

The pale lines are the sun world, fourth start at the same round since its founders: in grey, and only on the charts of a share or a rate, where a band of this world can be read against a rig of that one. Each device counts its own rounds, so the seven lines are seven clocks. Numbers that only the timed readings carry begin where tracking began. Marks are deploys and crashes; point at one to read it.

  3. Nov 13 13:35 UTCstop
    The fifth start is stopped cleanly and kept; a test of a pi oracle runs on the five cards

    On the owner's word ("restart the cluster with the pie oracle test") all seven nodes were asked to store their regions and stop between 13:28:43 and 13:34:55 UTC. Every node stopped cleanly; the data stays where it is and the start can go on from these rounds. Since 13:38 UTC (rig B) and 13:41 UTC (rig A) the five graphics cards run a test that is not part of this start: rules 8 with an oracle that reads the decimal digits of pi off the bytes of each program and gives a stretch of land less light the further it is behind its region's best. Each card is a world of its own with its own setting, one of them without the oracle as the control. The processors compute no world in the test. Nothing of the test is on the tracker's pages.

  4. Nov 13 11:19 UTCdeploy
    All seven bands run again, with a night that comes from the machine

    From 11:11 to 11:19 UTC all seven nodes were stopped cleanly, given new code and started again; rig B's three card nodes went on from the rounds at which their guards had stopped them the evening before. New with this code is a night by rest, the user's idea of this morning: if the cards heat up they are cooled down, with less energy, and this shows as night. A node now looks at its machine after every round, taking the hottest reading since its last look. On rig B night falls on its bands when any of its graphics cards has been at 77 degrees, or when the kernel counts a single new bus error. A node at night waits after each round, so that its device works a fifth of the time; its meter reads on, and since under rules 7 a band's light is what its device draws, the band gets about a quarter of its daylight. Day breaks at the look after a rest, five minutes at the earliest, when the machine has cooled. Rig A's limits are far above where it runs, so it has no night. The limits are settings of the machines, no rule of the world, and the rules' fingerprint is unchanged. Two rehearsals on rig B's three cards came first (no bus error in 58 minutes at or near full power), and two reviews, which found among other things that a look at one moment misses the heat (a card is eight degrees cooler seconds after its work) and that a stuck reading of a card could have left a node hanging. The first night of the running world fell at 11:19:50 UTC, four minutes after the start: the processor's band and two of the three card bands of rig B went dark within 25 seconds of each other, and the processor cooled from 64 to 35 degrees in three minutes. What a night does to a band was measured at once: under a quarter of its light, more than half of its organisms starve in the first night round (6.28 million to 2.68 million in the band of the hottest card), and in the rehearsal a band was back at nine tenths of its number three day rounds after dawn. The guard beside each node has a third case as well: if the kernel counts bus errors fast, it stops a card's node cleanly while the machine can still be reached.

  12. Nov 13 08:53 UTCrestart
    Four of the seven bands run again; rig B's three cards wait for a guardrail

    At 08:53 UTC the three nodes of rig A and the processor's node of rig B were started again. Each went on from the round at which its guard had stopped it the evening before; nothing had been lost. The three card nodes of rig B stay stopped for now. Both times rig B lost the link to its chipset, its three cards and its processor had run at full power for a while, its lowest card at 81 to 84 degrees with its fan at its limit, and the kernel had counted bus errors by the thousand in the minutes before. With the cards off, its processor's node runs at 54 degrees and the kernel counts no error. So the cards come back when two things are in place: a node that rests its device when the machine runs too hot, which under rules 7 makes its band dark (the user's idea: a night that comes from the real machine), and a guard that stops the card nodes on the first fast run of bus errors, while the machine can still be reached. Both are built and are being rehearsed on rig B's cards beside the running world.

    rig A processor round 241, rig A 4090 round 287, rig A 4080 round 277, rig B processor round 322 · commit 9a22463 · RUNTIME
  13. Nov 13 08:48 UTCfinding
    Why both rigs went off the network: rig A's network chip lost its link, rig B lost everything behind its chipset a second time

    Both machines were switched off and on at 08:33 UTC on 13 November and answered again from 08:37. Their kernel logs give two different causes. On rig A, at 17:33:25 UTC, the network chip dropped off its own PCI Express link and the kernel detached it. The 4090 behind the same chipset, the drive and everything else worked on, and the machine logged no bus error at all. Link power saving is switched on for that chip. On rig B the course of 13:50:59 UTC repeated itself at 16:50:09: correctable bus errors on every device behind the chipset and on the link between processor and chipset, rising from a few lines a minute to 2,600 a minute within 20 to 50 minutes, then a fatal error the kernel could not recover from, and everything behind the chipset gone until the power was cycled. There was not one such line in the six days before 12 November. Both times the three cards and the processor had run at full power for 18 to 40 minutes, the third card at 83 to 84 degrees with its fan at 99%. Link power saving is off on every link of rig B, so that is not the cause there; heat is the leading explanation and is not proven. Rig B's three card nodes stay stopped until their guard can stop them on the first bus errors, before the link fails.

  24. Nov 12 17:33 UTCcrash
    Rig A went off the network; its guards stopped its three nodes cleanly at 17:43 UTC, and the fifth start stood still

    Rig A stopped answering at 17:33 UTC, 43 minutes after rig B. Its readings went on every minute as well. By them its network port stayed up, but passed its last bytes between 17:33:00 and 17:34:00 and not one after that, in either direction, until the machine was switched off and on the next morning. Its guards found at 17:33:43 that nothing answered and stopped its three nodes cleanly at 17:43 UTC: the processor's at round 241, the 4090's at round 287 and the 4080's at round 277, with 57.8 million organisms in 138,194 inhabited regions. With that every node of the fifth start was stopped, each cleanly and by its guard, 95 minutes after the start. The world stood still with 87.4 million organisms in 223,883 inhabited regions until four of its nodes were started again at 08:53 UTC on 13 November.

    rig A processor round 227, rig A 4090 round 271, rig A 4080 round 262 · the tracker, from the readings and the guards' logs

  26. Nov 12 16:50 UTCcrash
    Rig B went off the network again; its guards stopped its four nodes cleanly at 17:00 UTC

    Rig B stopped answering at 16:50 UTC, 1 h 54 min after it had been switched on again. The machine itself ran on, and its own readings went on every minute: its network port was up at 16:50:00 and no port was up from 16:51:00 until the machine was switched off and on the next morning. Its four guards found at 16:50:14 that nothing answered, waited their ten minutes and stopped its four nodes cleanly at 17:00 UTC: the processor's at round 322, the three cards' at rounds 183, 177 and 179, with 29.6 million organisms in 85,689 inhabited regions between them. From 16:52 UTC on nothing arrived at any of the four any more, not even from each other, and by 17:00 the travellers waiting for a link had risen from about 8,000 to 122,000; every link was still called up. Rig A's three nodes ran on and called their links to rig B down within twenty minutes.

    rig A processor round 164, rig A 4090 round 198, rig A 4080 round 191, rig B processor round 303, rig B 3060a round 166, rig B 3060b round 160, rig B 3060c round 161 · the tracker, from the readings and the guards' logs

  28. Nov 12 16:10 UTCstart
    The fifth start began under rules 7: seven devices in a ring

    Every processor and every graphics card of the two machines is now a world of its own: seven bands of land in a ring, 286,720 regions in all, each with its own founder. The light of a band is the electricity its device really draws, read every round, so the world starts in twilight and brightens as it fills. After 70 seconds: 18,727 inhabited regions, 5.0 million organisms, 725 of 1,056 watts, every link between the seven up. Before the start the engines, all five cards and the scripts that run the world were checked, and all seven nodes were started, stopped and resumed once on test data. Each node has a guard that stops it cleanly if its machine runs out of memory or loses its network.
